title: How Invasive Rats Mess with Coral Reef Food Webs
author: Devin Reese
text: Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisementEnvironmentHow Invasive Rats Mess with Coral Reef Food WebsIt’s not always a bad thing, thoughDRBy Devin Reese7:00 AM CDT on August 3, 2026Add Nautilus to GoogleIt’s well-known that invasive rats can change island ecosystems. They eat eggs and chicks of ground-nesting birds, and gobble up small animals like lizards and beetles as well. It’s only when rats are removed from islands, such as Lord Howe Island in Australia or the Caribbean island of Redonda, that biodiversity begins to rebound. Subscribe to skip adsFeatured VideoPowered By 10 This Earth-Sized Planet Was Found Orbiting a Tiny StarShareNextStayNow, a recent study in the journal Ecology reports that ecological impacts of rats on islands extend far beyond their terrestrial habitats. Led by biologists at Lancaster University in the United Kingdom and the University of Texas, the study quantified the impacts of introduced rats on coral reefs near islands in the Indian Ocean. Black rats (Rattus rattus) were introduced several hundred years ago to these islands that otherwise have no direct human impacts. A previous study showed densities of seabirds to be about 760 times greater on rat-free islands, resulting in an influx of nutrients from bird droppings that “fertilize” the surrounding reefs. As such, the corals grew faster and supported more fish.Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisement
